newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia still not a done deal.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia still not a done deal.

text.p: The Bosnian war, Europe's worst in a half century, ended one year ago on Thursday in Dayton, Ohio with the initialling of an historic peace accord.
Today the guns are silent and the country's Moslem, Croat and Serb armies are back in their barracks. Casualties among NATO-led forces deployed to seal the deal have been few.
So why this nagging feeling that Bosnia's peace process could still unravel?
"I'm deeply worried about three things," a senior western diplomat in Sarajevo told Reuters this week.
"(Those are) war criminals, freedom of movement and the return of refugees. Unless we move to be more assertive in these areas, to ensure real results, Dayton could end up a colossal failure."
The Dayton agreement was sold to sceptical Bosnian Moslems and to the world as more than just an end to war.
Beyond the military goal of separating and confining the country's military forces, which NATO managed handily, Dayton promised peace with justice.
War criminals indicted by a U.N. tribunal were to be sent to the Hague for trial.
The ethnic partition of Bosnia was to be overturned and the country rebuilt with full freedom of movement and the right of refugees to return to their homes.
A year later diplomats, soldiers and aid workers agree that Bosnia's reality falls far short of Dayton's rhetoric.
What was billed as an administrative boundary between Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and its Serb republic now functions as a de facto border.
Freedom of movement is severely restricted and large swathes of Bosnia are dangerous no-go areas for those who would be ethnic minorities in them.

Within the federation Moslems and Croats are often at one another's throats. The one city they share, Mostar, is effectively partitioned despite hundreds of millions of dollars in European Union financial and administrative assistance.
There is no telephone or postal service between the two entities and no common vehicle registration system.

The U.N. estimates that only 250,000 of Bosnia's 2.5 million refugees and displaced people were able to return home in 1996, virtually none of them across the country's increasingly rigid ethnic borders.
There has been sporadic gunfire between Moslems trying to return home across those borders and Serbs who fought a war for "pure" ethnic territory.
Mysterious night-time explosions have destroyed hundreds of houses on Serb territory before Moslems could reoccupy them.
U.N. officials report that only seven of 75 indicted war criminals are now in custody at the Hague.
The Bosnian Serb republic, where most of the remainder live -- some still holding positions of public responsibility -- rejects the U.N. tribunal's jurisdiction and refuses to extradite indictees.
Despite these problems, critics who dismiss the peace process as the world's most expensive ceasefire are surely premature.
"If we fail in Bosnia the failure would be so great that I believe the international community will yet recognise its responsibility and do the right thing," a U.S. NATO officer said.

"In my opinion the issue of war criminals is peripheral to providing military security for freedom of movement and refugee returns, without which this country will be partitioned. Taking the risk to provide that security is a political decision."

"To deploy into a lethal zone and expect no casualties -- indeed, to effectively order that no casualties be taken -- is wrong because it undermines military and civilian policy-making at the highest levels."
Analysts say that, a year after Dayton, the international dilemma in Bosnia is the same as when the country was at war.

Contributors to the multinational force here -- once the U.N. and now NATO -- must agree the mix of military muscle and diplomacy needed to move the process forward rather than to preserve the status quo.
Then they must agree to take the attendant risks despite domestic political environments where, in the United States especially, NATO combat deaths could spell catastrophe.
